activities.caption: file each operation under its physical meaning
activities.name: vmOpSort

config.prompt: File each operation under its physical meaning:

items.label: B − A is the vector that takes you from A to B
−v flips the arrow through the origin

config.why: Each operation has a physical meaning worth keeping in view — combining winds, stretching forces, finding displacements.

activities.anchor: a vector and a point are the same thing
activities.caption: true or false — points and displacements
activities.name: vmPointJudge

config.statement: Adding a point to a point is meaningless while subtracting two points is perfectly fine — the difference of two locations is a genuine displacement.
config.why: A vector is a displacement with no fixed home; drawing it from the origin is a convention, not a property.

config.prompt: |v| = √(x² + y²). For v = (3, 4) it is √25 = 5. What is |u| for u = (1, −2)?
config.why: √(1 + 4) = √5 ≈ 2.24 — and dividing by it gives the unit vector, the way to express 'direction only'.
config.context: a force of 50 N along (3, 4) decomposes as 50 × (3/5, 4/5) = (30, 40) N

activities.anchor: u · v = x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ converts two vectors into one number
activities.caption: fill the blanks — reading the dot product's sign
activities.name: vmDotCloze

config.text: The dot product converts two vectors into one number that measures alignment: positive means an %%0%% angle between them, negative an obtuse angle, and exactly zero means %%1%% — test (1, 2) against (−2, 1): −2 + 2 = 0.
config.hint: One sign means 'less than 90°'; zero means the other measuring instrument's favourite answer.

config.prompt: One of these claims about the collinearity proof is wrong — click it:
lines: Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other.
Since QR = 2·PQ, all three lie on one line — no need to check they share a point.
config.correction: You must also check they share the point Q — parallel displacements alone do not force collinearity.
config.why: Since QR = 2·PQ and they share the point Q, all three lie on one line.

activities.anchor: The first diagonal's midpoint is ½(A + B)
activities.caption: two ways to bisect a parallelogram — drag the divider
activities.name: vmDiagCompare

config.prompt: Proving the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other — drag the divider:

before.label: diagram
before.text: draw the parallelogram and eyeball the diagonals — works only in the plane

after.label: components
after.text: both midpoints compute to ½(A + B) — four symbols, no diagram required

config.why: The component proof works for parallelograms in 3D or 10D just as well — dimension-independence is the quiet superpower.

activities.anchor: the matrix's <strong>columns are the images of the basis
activities.caption: pair each transformation with its matrix
activities.name: vmMatrixMatch

config.prompt: Pair each linear transformation with its 2×2 matrix:
config.why: The columns are the images of the basis vectors — once known, the image of any vector follows by one multiplication, because M(3, 2) = 3·M(e₁) + 2·M(e₂).

activities.anchor: rotate the plane 90° then reflect in
activities.caption: does order matter?
activities.name: vmOrderBranch

config.root: Rotate the plane 90° then reflect in the x-axis, versus reflect then rotate — applied to (1, 0). Do they agree?

choices.label: Yes — both end at (0, −1)
choices.feedback: No: rotation then reflection gives (0, −1); reflection then rotation gives (0, 1) — the matrices genuinely differ.

choices.label: No — order is sacred because multiplication is composition of motions
choices.feedback: Right — and geometry told us so before the algebra did.

choices.label: Yes, because matrix multiplication is associative
choices.feedback: Associativity lets you regroup brackets: (AB)C = A(BC); it says nothing about swapping order.

no.text: Almost no matrices commute — MN ≠ NM in general.

right.text: The exception worth remembering: a matrix commutes with its own powers, and R⁴ = I for the quarter-turn.

config.why: Multiplication is composition of motions and motions do not commute.

activities.caption: drop the marker — the area scale factor
activities.name: vmDetPlace

config.prompt: For M = [ a b ; c d ], det M = ad − bc. A reflection has det = −1. What is det M for M = [ 3 1 ; 1 2 ]?
config.why: 6 − 1 = 5 — any shape's area is multiplied by 5, and det = 0 would mean the plane crushed onto a single line, with no inverse.

config.prompt: Rebuild the inverse-matrix solution — what comes first:
items: Write M = [ 3 1 ; 1 2 ] and compute det M = 5
config.why: The matrix view finds the crossing point by un-transforming the output — and det = 5 promised the lines were not parallel.
